articles.title: The Royal Tenenbaums
articles.description: A precise and tender family comedy about old wounds, eccentric rituals, failed promise, and the difficult work of repair.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: The Royal Tenenbaums is framed as more than a stylish ensemble comedy. The listing copy now points to the page's focus on family distance, Wes Anderson's precise visual language, Royal's uneasy return, and the film's mixture of deadpan humor, sadness, and fragile forgiveness.

articles.title: TÁR
articles.description: A psychological character study about power, public reputation, and moral compromise in the world of classical music.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: This note focuses on TÁR as a tense study of authority and self-protection. It looks at Cate Blanchett's performance, Todd Field's precise direction, and the way the film turns concert halls and institutional polish into a setting for ethical collapse.

articles.title: The Banshees of Inisherin
articles.description: A darkly comic island story about friendship, rejection, loneliness, and the strange pride that turns hurt into violence.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: The Banshees of Inisherin starts with a friendship ending and lets the wound widen slowly. The metadata now reflects the page's focus on dialogue, isolation, the bleak Irish landscape, and the way comedy and cruelty sit uncomfortably close together.

articles.title: Aftersun
articles.description: A quiet, memory-shaped father-daughter story about love, distance, and the sadness that becomes clearer with time.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: Aftersun is presented as an intimate film about memory rather than a simple holiday story. The expanded copy points to the page's emphasis on Paul Mescal's restrained performance, warm visual texture, and the emotional gap between what a child sees and what an adult later understands.

articles.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once
articles.description: A multiverse film that turns chaotic invention into a tender story about family, identity, and acceptance.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: Everything Everywhere All at Once is summarized as both spectacle and emotional family drama. The longer listing text connects its visual play, multiverse structure, and rapid humor with the more grounded questions of belonging, love, and how people stay connected across difference.

articles.title: Birdman
articles.description: A formally restless look at fame, ego, artistic validation, and the pressure to stay relevant.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: Birdman is framed around performance, recognition, and the anxiety of being trapped by an old success. The expanded metadata reflects the page's attention to the apparent single-take style, Michael Keaton's vulnerable lead performance, and the film's sharp divide between art, entertainment, and approval.

articles.title: Fargo
articles.description: A snowbound crime story where greed, absurdity, and violence are measured against the stubborn decency of Marge Gunderson.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: Fargo is framed as more than a clever crime film. The review focuses on the Coen Brothers' balance of deadpan humor and violence, Frances McDormand's quietly moral performance as Marge Gunderson, and the snowbound landscape that turns ordinary greed into something stark and unforgettable.

articles.title: Three Colors Trilogy
articles.description: A philosophical trilogy that studies liberty, equality, and fraternity through color, coincidence, grief, and connection.
articles.author: Ugur Kostak
articles.content: Three Colors Trilogy is described as three connected films that each stand alone while contributing to a larger meditation on human connection. The metadata highlights Kieslowski's use of color, fate, and moral choice without reducing the trilogy to a simple theme summary.
